newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Moldova on backburner for westward-looking Romania.
newsitem.headline: Moldova on backburner for westward-looking Romania.

text.p: Romania will keep a close eye on this weekend's presidential election in neighbouring Moldova, but ties with ethnic kin there are on the backburner as Bucharest looks west towards NATO and the European Union.
The foreign policy priorities of centrist Emil Constantinescu, who was sworn in as Romanian president on Friday, look in the opposite direction from the former Soviet republic.

For Romania, where living standards have fallen behind eastern European neighbours Hungary and Poland, Moldova is a poor relation to which it can offer little succour. Yet Bucharest is still paying close attention to Sunday's vote.

"The president of Moldova can influence the process which might lead to a common future," said Radu Vasile, spokesman of the National Peasant Party, backbone of the centrist alliance which ousted ex-communists in this month's general election.
Only a tiny minority in either state, however, now talks of building a greater Romania, incorporating most of Moldova plus other former Romanian territory now in western Ukraine.
"Moldova's economy is dependent on Moscow. We have our problems, we don't need theirs," said a top Romanian analyst.
Sunday's winner, President Mircea Snegur or parliament chairman Petru Lucinschi, can influence Chisinau's foreign outlook -- east to Moscow or west with closer ties to Romania.

Snegur, backed by groups seeking closer ties with Bucharest, seems to be running neck and neck with Lucinschi, who plays on anxieties that the landlocked state, which depends on Russia for much of its energy, will be submerged in a greater Romania.
The two countries have more than a border in common.
Moldova is made up mostly of land seized from Romania under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact. Nearly two-thirds of its 4.3 million people are ethnic Romanians who call themselves Moldovans.
Fear of being subsumed into Romania prompted the 700,000 Slavic speakers of the Dnestr region to break away from Moldova in 1990. Hundreds died in a civil war over the issue in 1992.

A senior Romanian diplomat said that whatever the outcome of the vote, the new leaders had to "establish immediate contacts and relaunch gradual economic and cultural integration" between what both Bucharest and Chisinau call their "sister states".
Constantinescu, an academic with no political career under Communism, unlike his predecessor Ion Iliescu, acknowledges his sentimental links to Moldova, where he was born 57 years ago.
Without questioning existing borders, he called during his campaign for recognition of the wrong done to Romanians in 1939.
Both Romania and Moldova have favoured gradual economic and cultural integration, rather than a quick, German-style merger. And it is likely to remain so whoever wins on Sunday.

"Changing existing borders is out of the question," said Vasile, elected deputy chairman of the Romania parliament's upper house this week. "A common future for Romania and Moldova lies only with European integration."
Romania has yet to sign treaties with any of the three former Soviet republics to its immediate east -- Ukraine, Moldova and Russia. Talks have stumbled over the legacy of 1939.
Bucharest wants some acknowledgement of its lost territory. Russia and Ukraine say both sides should bury the past.
Strategic interests make signing a treaty with Ukraine more urgent for Romania than one with Russia, let alone Moldova.
"There is a good chance the treaty with Ukraine will be signed shortly, which will boost our chances of integration into Western structures, especially our goal of admission into NATO," Vasile said.
